asDecan.p: Every sign gets split into three ten-degree slices, called decans, and each slice has its own planet and its own small card. Your Sun is in the first ten degrees of Aries, and in the old Golden Dawn order that slice belongs to Mars. Mars already rules Aries, so here the sign's own planet is running the sign's own opening stretch, with nobody else's taste mixed in. That's why astrologers call it Aries at its most Aries. The next slice along belongs to the Sun, the Three of Wands, which is warmer and a bit keener to be seen. The last is Venus, the Four, which likes company and a finished house. Yours has neither of those softeners. The Emperor is your Sun card, the broad picture of Aries, and the Two of Wands is the finer grain inside it. Have a look at the man on the castle wall with the little globe in his hand. He's already holding one world and he's looking hard at the next one.

You usually know what you want before you know why, and you've gone for it before the why turns up. In a meeting where everyone's circling the problem, you're the one who says 'right, so who's doing what', and half the room is relieved and the other half is a bit put out. At the café you've ordered while your friend is still reading the specials board. A group chat trying to pick a weekend for the trip can go on for days, and by the second evening you've lost patience and just booked the place. A Sunday with nothing planned is fine for about an hour, then you're repainting the back fence. And a queue that isn't moving, you feel that in your legs. None of it is rudeness. Mars in its own first degrees just leaves very little gap between wanting a thing and doing it.

The gift people don't expect is how clean you are to deal with. There's no hidden version of you keeping score in the background. If you're annoyed it's on your face, and ten minutes later it's gone, and the people who work with you learn they never have to guess where they stand. That's rarer than it sounds. The other thing is how well you take a no. A job you didn't get, a pitch that got knocked back, a date who never texted. You feel it hard for an evening, and by the next morning you've usually applied for two more things. I've seen an early Aries Sun get passed over for a promotion on a Friday and be halfway through a business plan by Monday lunchtime. Mars at home doesn't sit in a loss for long, which makes you very hard to discourage.

The less obvious trouble is that your courage is mostly about doing. Give you a fire to put out or a bully to stand up to and you're first in. Give you something that can't be fixed by moving, a friend who's grieving and just needs you to sit there, a partner who wants to talk about how they feel with no plan at the end of it, and you get fidgety and start offering solutions nobody asked for. Sometimes you'll pick a fight because a fight is at least something to do. There's also a habit of living one step ahead of your own life. You're so busy with the next thing that the people who've been there all along start to feel like part of the furniture. Your mum, or your oldest mate, can go three months without hearing from you, and you honestly didn't notice the time go.

When something goes wrong your first move is to do something, fast. The redundancy email arrives and within the hour you've updated your CV and messaged six people. A breakup, and you're at the gym at six the next morning going much too hard. That first burst is useful and it gets real things done. A week on it's usually turned into irritability. You're short with the kids, you swear at the driver in front, and you're sleeping badly because your body's been in go mode for days with nowhere to put it. The people near you get the heat without the explanation, which isn't fair on them. What actually helps is something physical and hard enough to burn off the Mars, a long run, a cold swim, splitting wood, and then one person you'll let see you sad once the anger's gone.

Aries is the first sign and Libra sits opposite it, so with the Sun this early in Aries you're often drawn to people who are good at exactly the things you skip. The ones who ask how everyone's feeling, who take a week to decide on a couch, who notice the tone of a message. It can drive you up the wall, and it's often who you need. You fall quickly and you say so, which is lovely at the start. What partners find harder is that you show love by doing. You fix the tap, you book the trip, you turn up with the car when it's raining. You're less good at the long, slow talk about where the two of you are headed, and you can hear their wanting to talk as a complaint. It usually isn't one. Try staying in the chair a bit longer than feels comfortable.

You work best when there's something to win or something that doesn't exist yet. Launches, start-ups, turnarounds, the first month of a new team, emergency work, sport, anything with a starting gun. You're usually the one who drafts the proposal nobody asked for and sends it to the boss at nine on a Thursday night. What wears you down is maintenance. The fourth year of the same system, the admin that follows a big win, the meeting to plan the meeting. If you can, set things up so someone who likes finishing picks up where you leave off, and make sure they get the credit, because an early Aries can forget that person exists. Working for yourself suits a lot of people with this decan. Just be honest with yourself about who's going to do the invoicing.

At twenty this slice of Aries tends to be all launch. Three courses started, a band, a move interstate on a week's notice, and a fair few arguments you'd have won if you'd waited to hear the other half. That's normal, and plenty of it works out. By the mid-thirties most have noticed how many things they began and then handed off, and the ones who do well pick one or two to actually carry through, often a business, a family, or a skill they've kept at for a decade. The temper tends to cool faster too, even if it still lights just as quickly. In the fifties this decan often becomes the person younger people ring when they need a push. You're still quick off the mark and still twitchy in long queues, but you choose your starts with more care, and people notice.

Pick one thing you started in the last year and left half done. The course, the garden bed, the side project, the email to your cousin. Set a timer for twenty-five minutes and work only on the next piece of it, even if it's dull. When the timer goes, write the piece after that on a sticky note and put it where you'll see it in the morning. Do this on three separate days before you let yourself begin anything new.
